To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the dOdiatom data of Lake Ladoga reveal a pronounced Holocene cooling trend, with the highest dOdiatom around 6.1–4.1 cal.ka BP.

1) Lake Ladoga was a freshwater lake during the Holocene, 2) dOdiatom is an excellent proxy for Holocene lake-level changes, 3) the Holocene ThermalMaximum was reflected in relatively high dOdiatoms, 4) the Middle to Late Holocenecooling was reflected in relatively low dOdiatoms and 5) the Little Ice Age was the coolest period during the Holocene.

the Holocene hydrology of Lake Ladoga has been characterized by a persistent freshwater reservoir, with an early outflow opening and overall high d Odiatom around +33.7& reflecting a persistent evaporative system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a better understanding of the Holocene climate and environmental variability of the Lake Ladoga region, which is of particular interest in the context of the current climate change.
the Holocene hydrology of a large lake in the Baltic Sea drainage basin, which is important for a better understanding of climate–lake interactions in the region.
the development of Lake Ladoga as an important freshwater reservoir in the European Arctic and its response to climate change.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Lake Ladoga was a relatively stable freshwater lake with a persistent evaporative regime throughout the Holocene, with only a slight increase in evaporation during the Little Ice Age.

Lake Ladoga is a freshwater lake with a rather persistent hydrological regime, which is sensitive to climatic forcing, but also prone to local hydrological changes, such as river inflows and outflows.
the dOdiatom data reflect the combined effects of climate change, catchment dynamics, and lake-level changes, which all have an influence on the isotopic composition of lake water.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Lake Ladoga was an evaporative lake with a persistent water level throughout the Holocene, and that the lake-level variations were mainly driven by changes in precipitation and evaporation.

Holocene climate variability in Lake Ladoga is primarily driven by the combined effect of solar insolation and the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO), which is in line with the results obtained for the Baltic Sea.

Lake Ladoga was a rather stable lake system during the Holocene, and that the Holocene hydrology of Lake Ladoga was controlled by the interplay of the local climate, the Neva River inflow and the lake outflow.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Lake Ladoga isotope record provides a valuable addition to existing Holocene climate records from the region.

the Lake Ladoga isotope hydrology is a sensitive tool for reconstructing Holocene climate change in the Baltic Sea basin, and the Lake Ladoga diatom isotope data can be used as a proxy for the reconstruction of the hydrological variability of the Baltic Sea.
dOdiatom of diatom frustules can be successfully employed to study Holocene lake-level changes in large and deep lakes.
